title: Startup path latency and kernel-cache effects
content:
Summary:
This note collects experiments that isolate the "startup" codepath overheads (first-request behaviour) and the effect of various kernel / driver caches on apparent latency for short-text generation workloads. Goal is to produce deterministic mitigations that reduce first-token and prefill latency variance across SKUs (A100 / H100 / L40S) and across cloud instance families and driver/CUDA versions.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Many production P50/P95 SLO misses are coming from cold or semi-warm workers. Warm token latency is fine, but first request or after-a-long-idle is highly variable.
- Hypothesis: multiple layered caches (user-space JIT/cubin caches, driver-level kernel module state, GPU power/P-state transitions, CUDA context/kernel launch caches) cause most of the extra tail. Different SKUs + driver stacks have different magnitudes.

Test matrix (high level):
- SKUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB (cloud P3/P4 analogs), H100 80GB, L40S.
- Instances: AWS p4de (A100), GCP a3 or custom (A100), GCP h100 (H100), Azure L40S sku.
- CUDA/driver combos: CUDA 11.8 + driver 525.x, CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.x, CUDA 12.2 + driver 547.x (representative sets).
- Framework: PyTorch 2.2 + custom inference runtime binary (serving-runtime v0.89).
- Workload: short prompts (prefill length 32, decode length 16), batched size 1 and 4. Measurements: first-token latency (time from HTTP accept to first byte streamed), prefill completion, and post-prefill decode latency.

Micro-experiments and instrumentation:
- Instrumented startup traces that record timestamps for: process start, load-shared-libs, cuInit, cuDeviceGet, cuCtxCreate, cuModuleLoad / cuModuleLoadData, cuLaunchKernel(s) for prefill kernels, cuBLAS/cuDNN first-call overhead, nvmlInit, and GPU power state change detected via NVML.
- eBPF hooks (user probes) to capture open()/dlopen() of libcudart.so and libcublas.so to check lazy-loading behavior.
- Kernel-level sampling to detect page-fault vs. CPU work before GPU launches.
- Micro-benchmark: run a small kernel that exercises matmul/attention kernels to populate kernel caches; report its latency as a surrogate for kernel-cache heat.

Representative results (aggregated, median/p95 in ms):
- A100 (CUDA 11.8, driver 525):
  - cold-first-token median: 260 ms, p95: 410 ms
  - warmed-first-token median: 14 ms, p95: 28 ms
  - comments: NVML init + cuCtxCreate + first cuBLAS call accounted for ~150 ms of cold overhead. Kernel upload + module JIT (where present) added another 60–90 ms.
- H100 (CUDA 12.1, driver 535):
  - cold-first-token median: 190 ms, p95: 300 ms
  - warmed-first-token median: 11 ms, p95: 22 ms
  - comments: H100's driver stack appears to do fewer on-demand relocations on our binary kernels; cold overhead smaller but still non-trivial due to power-state transition in some instances.
- L40S (CUDA 12.2, driver 547):
  - cold-first-token median: 340 ms, p95: 520 ms
  - warmed-first-token median: 16 ms, p95: 36 ms
  - comments: L40S instances we tested have deeper power-saving ramps and slower PCIe initialization in the cloud SKU tested; kernel cache miss penalty also higher (probable driver or kernel variant mismatch).

Cross-driver observations:
- Moving from CUDA 11.8 -> 12.x reduced cold overhead on H100 in our runs by ~60 ms, but in a few A100 images showed no improvement. Driver+kernel pairing matters a lot.
- Some driver versions trigger on-the-fly PTX->SASS JIT for certain kernels we compile as cubin-with-ptx fallback. Removing PTX fallback (ship precompiled SASS for the architecture) eliminated ~30–70 ms of variability on A100 in our tests.

Root causes (evidence-backed):
1) Lazy runtime initialization: cuInit / cuDriverGetVersion / nvmlInit are non-negligible. They run once per process and frequently interleave with other start tasks, increasing tail when combined with I/O.
2) GPU power/performance state transitions: when GPU is at low P-state, first heavy kernel can trigger frequency ramps; detectable using NVML events and correlates with ~40–150 ms wasted time (SKU-dependent).
3) Kernel codepath population: driver-level caches and fallbacks (PTX->SASS JIT) are a major source. Preloading/provisioning precompiled kernels mitigates this.
4) dlopen and library lazy symbols: delays when libcudart or libcublas symbols are resolved on first call.
5) CPU-side page faults and memory-initialization work (zeroing, allocator warmups) show up as CPU time prior to GPU submission.

Practical mitigations we validated:
- Worker pre-warm routine (to run in the worker init path, before accepting requests):
  1) dlopen("libcudart.so") and an explicit cuInit() call.
  2) Create & keep one persistent CUDA context per worker thread/process and run a tiny matmul kernel to force kernel cache population and cuBLAS initialization.
  3) Pre-allocate large pinned buffer (a small KV cache allocation) to avoid first-call page faults.
  4) Touch GPU memory at known hot addresses to ensure mapping existence.
  5) Run an NVML call to set application clocks to preferred profile where allowed.
- Ship architecture-specific compiled kernels where possible (avoid runtime PTX JIT). For open models with dynamic kernels, include a lightweight kernel-priming binary in the Docker image.
- Keep a small pool of warm workers per node (1-2 warm processes) that are recycled on schedule to keep kernel caches hot.

Quantified impact of mitigations (same short-prompt workload):
- With pre-warm routine enabled and warm pool of 1:
  - A100: cold-first-token median dropped from 260 ms -> 70 ms, p95 410 -> 120 ms.
  - H100: 190 ms -> 60 ms median.
  - L40S: 340 ms -> 120 ms median (still higher than A100/H100 but much improved).
- Warm-path latencies were unchanged within noise. Cost of pre-warm: about +150–350 MB GPU memory and ~30–60 ms added to startup time per worker (acceptable tradeoff).

Operational notes / tradeoffs:
- Keeping workers warm increases static capacity consumption; need to balance against user-visible SLOs. For low-traffic customers, warm-pool size should be small but non-zero.
- Some cloud providers restrict clock overrides; our routine falls back gracefully.
- Shipping platform-level SASS binaries reduces portability; we need a CI step to generate multi-arch kernel artifacts and sign them.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Why is L40S consistently worse in our sample set? Hypothesis: cloud vendor firmware + PCIe/BIOS settings and driver image composition. Action: request a similar instance from another zone/provider and test identical driver image.
- Investigate whether kernel-cache eviction happens asynchronously (e.g., when multi-tenant noise evicts entries) and whether cross-process sharing is possible for our use-case.
- Measure long-idle resumption (minutes->hours) to find decay curves for kernel caches and power-state ramps.

Appendix: reproducibility checklist and commands (high level)
- Baseline script: scripts/bench/startup_bench.sh --sku A100 --cuda 11.8 --instance p4d --prompt-length 32 --trials 200
- Prewarm routine (pseudo):
  - dlopen libcudart -> cuInit(); cuDeviceGet(0); cuCtxCreate(); run tiny matmul kernel (64x64) using same cuBLAS handle; cudaMemcpy a single byte; create pinned allocation and write to it.
- Traces to capture: startup_trace.log (timestamps for each instrumented hook), nvml_events.log, bpf_open_traces.txt.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: finalize bench harness and land PR that adds pre-warm routine to worker init (PR link in artifacts).
- Marcus: spin cross-zone L40S test and collect reproducibility artifacts (JIRA-REND-4721).
- Diego: implement CI step to produce and archive architecture-specific kernel blobs.
- Priya: update runbook for Dedicated & Private (recommend warm-pool defaults and prewarm toggle).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an in-progress working doc; experimental numbers are from limited zones/instance images and should be considered directional. The mitigation recipe has been validated on our benchmark harness and reduced customer-facing cold-starts in internal dogfood runs.
- Please suggest other probe points to instrument (kernel load events, driver syscalls we missed) and any additional SKUs we should add to the matrix.
